To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the pace of human life has accelerated, and 2) the pace of nature has remained constant.

(1) the pace of social time has increased over the last 200 years; (2) this acceleration is due to a combination of factors, including the development of the industrial revolution, the development of the capitalist economy and the development of the welfare state; and (3) the increase in the pace of social life has had a number of consequences, including a greater emphasis on time and time management, an increase in the number of time-saving devices and the development of time-saving techniques
the pace of social life has increased dramatically over the past 150 years and that there is no evidence that this trend has yet been reversed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social and political implications of the `great divide' which exists between nature and human society.
the ways in which social and natural processes intersect and interact.
the relationship between the body and the environment and how this relationship is mediated by the body and the social.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nature and society are both `in time' and that the `natural' pace of nature is a human construction.
the `great divide' between nature and society is not as great as we have been led to believe, and is certainly not as great as the `great divide between the natural sciences and the human sciences'.
the `natural' and `social' are inextricably linked and that, therefore, any attempt to distinguish them is futile.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to create a sociology of the natural body, in which we would include the natural body of human beings, the bodies of non-human animals and plants and the bodies of the earth itself.
the body is the most important site of social change, as it is the site where social change is first experienced.

we are trying to show that there are many different kinds of time, and that these different times have different properties, and that we are trying, in this book, to explore these different kinds of times, and to explore their properties, and also to explore the relationship between these different kinds of time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human capacity for change, and the plasticity of the body, are important in understanding the relationship of the human to nature.
the social and natural worlds are not separate, and that they are not even different. They are one and the same.
the human body is a key site through which the relationship between nature and society is played out, with implications for how we theorise the natural world.
